messages.author: 8c6a877154df740e
messages.subject: model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
parts:
Dear all,

in my understanding, WAIC and (PSIS) LOO are metrics for model selection.

However, it happens that PSIS-LOO can also be used as a model diagnostics since if the measured LOO tail exponents are large it means that there are possibly influential observations and that the model is not robust (so it might be overfitting those); see also my previous post (and answers) on this mailing list.
So PSIS-LOO could be an informative tool in itself even if we are not comparing models.

Is this usage of PSIS-LOO appropriate, or is it somewhat dodgy? e.g., could I mention it in a paper as suggestive evidence for issues in a model?
(and are there references for specifically this usage -- perhaps this?)

Secondly -- this is more speculative.
I understand that there are theoretical advantages in performing continuous inference in a "large" model as opposed to discrete model selection.
(In the "large" model, specific hypotheses are identified by sub-regions in parameter space.)
However, how do I prevent overfitting / increase generalizability -- that is, how do I check my priors -- if I have a single "large model" and I don't want to go back to discrete model selection?

Best,
Luigi

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
parts:
Sure you could use it to identify issues but it's better not to stop there.  Try to plot the problematic observation to illustrate which model feature causes the issue.  You can get surprisingly specific answers that way about which aspect of a model to improve.

Krzysztof

messages.author: 8c6a877154df740e
messages.subject: Re: model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
parts:
OK, but suppose that I have a single "large" model and PSIS-LOO does not detect any major issue.
This means that all the LOO posteriors are "close enough" to the full posterior, which seems to be a good sign (i.e., at least the model is not overfitting to single observations).
To me, this seems informative in itself (of course then I can go and do predictive checks, but that's another point).

The question is, what do I report to provide partial evidence of (lack of) overfitting?
For a standard model selection, I would have some simpler and more complex models to compare against, and that's how the LOO-CV would play out.
But if you have a single model, it seems to me that PSIS-LOO would still allow you to say something.
First of all, is that acknowledged (any reference?); and second, what would be a good metric? (e.g., the maximum of the Pareto-fitted exponents, the largest IS weight, or something else based on the PSIS-LOO analysis)

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
parts:
All predictive measure are, and mathematically have to be, relative measures
of fit.  They provide no absolute measure of fit (because to do that you would 
need to know the true model). The use of these methods in isolation, particularly 
in posterior predictive checks, is always in reference to some default model (i.e.,
“this fit is so bad another model _has_ to be better”) but such comparisons can’t 
be quantified in any meaningful way.  So it’s easy to use these measures to
identity suspicious behavior and use that to motivate model improvements, but
they do not quantify any guarantee of your model being correct.

messages.author: 49e107cb0f8a3d27
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
parts:
Yes it’s true that diagnostics such as PPC’s are technically comparing against a true model. But I think the argument still holds—that PPC’s (or “model diagnostics” in general) are useful in light of not having another candidate model in mind. This is how Rubin (1981, 1984) phrases this.

Following this, I think Luigi’s question is also valid. That is, can PSIS-LOO be used as a model diagnostic in which we are assessing the goodness-of-fit without another candidate model in mind.

Dustin

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: model selection, diagnostics and generalizability
parts:
There is a lot of literature about using 
 - LOO log predictive densities aka conditional predictive ordinates (CPO) to detect influential observations 
 - and LOO cdfs aka probability integral transform (PIT) and to check calibration.
(some other test quantities have been also proposed)
These can be informative even if not comparing models.

PSIS-LOO computes in addition Pareto shape parameter estimates khats. These will tell, for example, whether CPOs and PITs can be trusted. khat values may sometimes indicate also influential observations, but there are also sensible models where khats can be large. For example, Gaussian process models tend to be difficult for importance sampling LOO even with PSIS and thus khats are often large, even if models are robust and not "overfitting" (overfitting is not well defined term).

Aki
